nodes.name: Water hyacinth & floating plants
nodes.desc: Floating and rooted aquatic plants that carpet the ponds and channels of the floodplain and feed grazers and snails.

nodes.name: Floodplain grasses
nodes.desc: Grasses of the seasonally flooded meadows. Capybara graze them, and when floodwater covers them they die back and rot in the water.

nodes.name: Acuri palm
nodes.desc: A palm whose very hard nuts are the main food of hyacinth macaws in the Pantanal. Collared peccaries and many birds also eat its fruit.

nodes.name: Bastardcedar
nodes.desc: A common tree of dry ground and forest islands whose fruit is eaten by peccaries and other forest animals.

nodes.name: Capybara
nodes.desc: A semi-aquatic grazer of grasses and water plants, living beside rivers and ponds. Jaguars, caimans and anacondas all prey on it.

nodes.name: Marsh deer
nodes.desc: A large deer of wet grassland and marshes. Jaguars take it when it is available.

nodes.name: Apple snails
nodes.desc: Wikipedia calls them a keystone group of the Pantanal. They eat dead plant matter in oxygen-poor floodwater and are food for many animals.

nodes.name: Curimbata & other detritus fish
nodes.desc: A migratory fish that feeds on fine organic matter. Most Pantanal fish are detritus eaters, which makes them a major food source for predators.

nodes.name: Collared peccary
nodes.desc: An omnivore of forest and scrub that eats palm nuts and fruit. Jaguars prey on it.

nodes.name: Hyacinth macaw
nodes.desc: A giant parrot that in the Pantanal feeds almost entirely on nuts of the acuri and bocaiuva palms.

nodes.name: Red-bellied piranha
nodes.desc: A predatory fish of lagoons and rivers. It is eaten by giant otters and jaguars.

nodes.name: Giant otter
nodes.desc: Family groups hunt fish, especially piranha and catfish. The Pantanal is a key habitat and its numbers have recovered there.

nodes.name: Jabiru
nodes.desc: A huge stork that wades in shallows for fish, snails, frogs and snakes, and also eats carrion and dead fish in dry spells.

nodes.name: Yacare caiman
nodes.desc: Eats snails and fish, and occasionally capybara. About 10 million live in the Pantanal after a ban on the skin trade.

nodes.name: Yellow anaconda
nodes.desc: A generalist that hunts in shallow wetland water for wading birds, apple snails, reptiles and mammals, mostly as floods recede.

nodes.name: Black vulture
nodes.desc: Soaring scavenger that cleans up carcasses, including capybara, across the wetland.

nodes.name: Jaguar
nodes.desc: Top predator. In the Pantanal it feeds on aquatic reptiles and fish, and also on capybara, deer and peccary, often hunting in the water.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Year-round warmth and light let floodplain plants grow fast when water is present.

nodes.name: Summer rains
nodes.desc: Most rain falls from November to March and feeds the rivers that flood the plain.

nodes.name: Seasonal flood
nodes.desc: Around 80 percent of the floodplain goes under water in the wet season, moving fish, nutrients and plant matter across the wetland.

nodes.name: Floodplain soil & nutrients
nodes.desc: Sediment and rotting plant matter left by the floods feed new growth.

nodes.name: Fungi & bacteria
nodes.desc: Rot the plants and animals that die in the water and soil and return nutrients, using up oxygen in the process.
